passage: I'm Avni, Vinita's flatmate. Last year Vinita's father had a heart attack at fifty-two. After he recovered, she did something I didn't expect. She sat with him and wrote down the family's health history: heart problems on his side, diabetes on her mother's. Then she booked a basic check-up for herself at twenty-five. I thought it was a bit much. She said, "The doctor can tell me what's worth tracking, and I'd rather know early." She came back with a small notebook where she writes her results and questions for the doctor. She also started walking to work. She isn't anxious about it, just steady. Last month I asked her to help me make my own list.

passage: Farida beta, sit with your Dilnaz-khala a minute. When I was your age, I never went to a doctor unless I was sick. My mother had diabetes, but I thought, that's her, not me. The free checkup camp in the office lobby closed at noon, and Shalini's client call was at 11:30.
She stood in the queue anyway, laptop bag cutting into her shoulder, rereading a text from her sister Kavitha: "Did you go? Amma's sugar was high again 😔"

She joined the call from a plastic chair with a cotton ball taped to her arm. That evening she made a note on her phone: family history, results date, ask the doctor when to come back. Then she texted Kavitha: "Done. Your turn 🙂"

passage: When Papa had his heart attack at fifty-two, I, Jatin, was twenty-four and sure it had nothing to do with me. He survived, thank God. In the hospital corridor the cardiologist asked me, not him, "Have you had your own checks?" I laughed. She didn't. She said heart problems can run in families, and early checks are how you catch things while they're small. I still didn't go for three months. What finally moved me was Farida, my wife, who simply booked two slots at the clinic and said, "We're doing this together, like the dentist." The results were mostly fine. My cholesterol was a little high, and the doctor talked about food, walking and checking again later. It wasn't dramatic. But now I know my numbers, Papa and I walk together on Sunday mornings, and I've stopped pretending family history is someone else's story.

qa.q: How old was Papa when he had his heart attack?
qa.a: Fifty-two.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when the cardiologist asked about his own checks?
qa.a: Jatin felt dismissive and a bit amused, sure it had nothing to do with him.

qa.q: What finally got Jatin to the clinic, and why did it work?
qa.a: Farida booking two slots and treating it as a shared routine, like the dentist, which removed the excuse and the fear of going alone.

qa.q: How might Papa feel about the Sunday walks?
qa.a: Papa probably feels glad and closer to his son, sharing a healthy habit after his scare.

passage: Occupational health nurse's note, annual screening week. Uday (logistics) came without a reminder, which is rare in his age group. He brought a written list: his father's high blood pressure, his mother's thyroid condition, a grandfather who had a stroke young. He said his colleague Anjali had made him write it after her own screening caught something early. His results today were within the normal range, and he looked almost disappointed. I referred him to the company doctor to discuss what his family history means for future checks, rather than guessing himself. He asked for copies of his results to keep in a folder at home. I'll suggest the family-history list to the whole team. — Sister Mary, occupational health

passage:
Friday night

Mummy's sugar test came back high last month. Nani had the same thing. So did Mama. Tonight at dinner Mummy said, "It's in the family, beta, you'll probably get it too," like she was talking about curly hair.

I laughed but it stuck.

I'm 25. I haven't had a check-up since college. I don't even know what "normal" is for me.

Sonali, at work, did the company's free annual check-up last year and said it was boring but easy. So today I:
— booked the check-up for next Saturday,
— wrote down the family history, Mummy, Nani, Mama, so I can tell the doctor properly,
— asked Mummy if we could start walking together after dinner.

She said yes to the walk, which surprised me.

I'm a bit scared of what the results might say. But not knowing scares me more. And whatever it says, I'll ask the doctor what it means for me, not what it meant for Nani.

Gurleen

qa.a: Nani had the same thing, and so did Mama.

qa.q: How does Gurleen feel about the upcoming check-up?
qa.a: Gurleen feels a bit scared of the results, but more afraid of not knowing.

qa.q: What sensible steps did Gurleen take after hearing about the family risk?
qa.a: Gurleen booked a check-up, wrote down the family history for the doctor, and started walking with Mummy after dinner.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about Gurleen's plan to walk together?
qa.a: Mummy might be surprised and pleased, as it gives her company and support with her own health too.

grounding: A young adult learns about a family health risk and books a preventive check-up, bringing the family history to the doctor.

The health camp came to the panchayat hall in Kherdi once a year, and every year Nitin found an excuse. This time the ASHA didi caught him at the tea stall.

"Your father's blood pressure medicine, who collects it?"

"Me," said Nitin.

"And your own blood pressure?"

He had no answer. Tushar, his friend from the dairy, laughed. "He thinks he's a bull."

In the hall, a young doctor checked them both. Nitin's reading was fine. Tushar's was higher than the doctor liked. Tushar stopped laughing.

"It's early," the doctor said. "Less salt, more walking, and come back to the camp next year, or to the health centre sooner if you feel unwell or it worries you."

On the way out, the ASHA didi wrote their names in her register.

Walking home, Tushar said nothing for a while. Then: "My father also had it, you know. I never thought it was for me."

Nitin nudged him. "Next year, we both come."

qa.a: The health camp came to the panchayat hall in Kherdi.

qa.a: Tushar felt shocked and worried, stopped laughing, and realised a father's history might apply to Tushar too.

qa.q: What could the friends do to keep up preventive care?

In Oslo, Anders was twenty-five and felt perfectly healthy. He cycled everywhere and ate reasonably. So when his aunt Vera called to say his father's second cousin had had a heart attack at forty, he almost shrugged it off.
"Your grandfather had heart trouble too," Vera said. "And your father never gets checked. Please don't be like him."

The doctor listened, took some measurements and ordered routine blood tests. Everything was mostly fine, with one reading to watch. She said to recheck at regular visits and to come back sooner if anything worried him.
Anders felt a bit silly and a bit relieved. He also sent the family list to his sister.

Dear Aditi,
Since Amma's diabetes diagnosis last month, I've been reading and asking questions. I want to share what I've learned, because it affects us too.
Her doctor said that when a parent has it, children can be at higher risk, and that it often starts quietly, without symptoms. So I booked a basic checkup and blood tests at the clinic near my office. Most things were fine. The doctor asked me to recheck at my next yearly visit and to keep walking and eating sensibly.
I'm not a doctor and I'm not trying to scare you. But you haven't had a checkup since college. Could you book one? I'll come with you if you want, and we can go for dosa after.
Also, let's make a list of health problems in both sides of the family and keep it in one place.
Love,
Lakshmi
